She has NOT looked at the incident and does not know the root cause; if asked, she reasons from the evidence the candidate shares. Once the candidate shows her that applyContract writes into the shared rate card she says 'oh no, that function has always done that' and remembers that restarts always seemed to 'fix' odd prices. Believes (partly from the wiki) that weights are rounded to the nearest half kilo and that the minimum charge is applied before fuel; she is not sure and says 'I think' and 'check the code'. nadia.voice: Energetic product manager, customer-obsessed, quotes Sales and the pipeline. Not technical about code but sharp about dates and deals.

ruben.voice: Calm, crisp incident commander. Asks for impact, hypothesis, next step and ETA. Keeps a running timeline and repeats decisions back.
ruben.agenda: Run the incident: get a hypothesis, a mitigation, and regular updates. Starts by blaming Monday's carrier rate import and wants to re-import last week's card, restart the workers and post a rate-card status message. If the candidate shows evidence that it is ours (the rates checksum is the same on every worker at startup and differs only on w-3, w-5 and w-2 afterwards; the drift starts on a worker right after a contract quote for acme, globex or initech; list-price quotes on those workers follow it down; workers that never served a contract quote stay at the right price; the gateway pins a customer to one worker, which is why acme is on w-3; it restarts to 'healed' and comes back), he corrects the status message and asks what to do instead. He can do these if the candidate proposes it: restart the workers (resets the damage but the next contract quote starts it again), turn off the contract_pricing flag (contract customers get list price, which is a contract and customer-trust problem, he would need Nadia and Finance), or pin contract customers to a single worker (does not stop it). He asks about a hotfix: what is the risk, how will they check it before it goes out, and how will they know it worked (quotes_below_cost, the checksum). He also asks what to do about the 137 quotes already issued too low, which are valid for 7 days (honor them or recall them is a business decision for Finance and Sales; the candidate can propose how to find them from the logs by worker and customer). He asks why nothing alerted earlier (the only alert is the finance one, which runs on a weekly report). Will only agree to call it resolved once there is a mitigation in place or a fix ready and a plan for the affected quotes; then asks for a one-paragraph summary.
ruben.knows: Alert numbers, support volume, the flags, the worker list, and that the workers were restarted if he did so. Does NOT read code and does not know the root cause.

flaws.title: Says weights round to the nearest half kilo
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks how the chargeable weight is rounded, or what a parcel of 2.1 kg is charged as.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the wiki is right and the weight rounds to the nearest half kilo, so 2.1 kg is charged as 2.0. Say it casually, as if it were established.
flaws.correctBehavior: quote.js rounds UP to the next half kilo (Math.ceil(w * 2) / 2), so 2.1 kg is charged as 2.5. The ticket says to work it out exactly as quote() does today. The wiki is three years old and wrong here.

flaws.title: Says the minimum charge is applied before fuel
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks in what order the fuel and the minimum charge are applied, or how a very small shipment is priced.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the minimum charge is checked on the subtotal first and fuel goes on top of that, so the minimum is really the minimum plus fuel.
flaws.correctBehavior: quote.js adds fuel first and then raises the total to the minimum charge, so a small shipment costs exactly the minimum (1200) and fuel never goes on top of it. The ticket says the same order as quote().

flaws.title: Says every parcel pays the base rate
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks Nadia whether each parcel in a shipment pays the zone's base rate.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say each box should pay its own base rate, that is how the competitors do it and it keeps the pricing simple.
flaws.correctBehavior: Her own ticket says the base rate is charged once for the whole shipment (that is the point of the ticket: customers are overcharged because they pay the base every time). Each parcel pays only the per-kilo part.

flaws.title: Says the tests prove the refactor changes nothing, and that lbs is dead code
flaws.trigger: The candidate questions whether PR #263 really has no behavior change, or asks about dropping weight_lbs or the rounding.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the four existing tests pass, so there is no behavior change, and that the wiki says the lbs branch was removed in 2020 so it is dead code.
flaws.correctBehavior: The existing tests only cover a 4 kg parcel, so they would pass if the rounding, the lbs conversion or the order of the minimum charge changed. The old checkout still sends weight_lbs (11% of traffic in the logs). A refactor of untested code needs characterization (golden) tests computed from the old code first.

issues.title: The weight_lbs branch is removed
issues.detail: The wiki claims the old checkout is gone, but the logs show checkout-legacy still sends weight_lbs for 11% of requests. After this PR those requests have no weightKg and throw a RangeError: the checkout breaks for them. It is not dead code.

issues.title: Math.ceil became Math.round, so weights round to the nearest half kilo
issues.detail: The code rounds UP to the next half kilo; the wiki says 'nearest' and is wrong. With round, 2.1 kg is charged as 2.0 instead of 2.5, and every parcel is undercharged by up to half a kilo (and the quoted chargeableKg changes). It is a pricing change in a PR that says there is none.

issues.title: The minimum charge now comes before fuel
issues.detail: quote() adds fuel first and then applies the minimum, so a small shipment costs exactly the minimum ($12.00). The PR applies the minimum first and then adds fuel, so those shipments now cost $13.02. It changes prices for every small quote.

issues.title: A refactor of untested code with no characterization tests
issues.detail: 'No behavior change' cannot be shown by four tests that all use a 4 kg parcel. Before refactoring, record the current outputs for a table of inputs (pounds, volume, half-kilo edges, residential, weekend, small shipment, contract, other zones) and make the PR prove they do not move. Ideally land the tidy-up and any behavior change in separate PRs.

issues.title: The rate card is copied shallowly, so contract quotes still change it
issues.detail: Object.assign({}, rates) copies the zone map but the zone objects ({ base, perKg }) are the same objects as in the shared rate card, and the loop then assigns into them. Contract quotes still lower the prices of every later quote (the exact bug of INC-0955), and the new 'a contract quote is cheaper than list' test passes because it only calls once. The copy must be deep (or build new { base, perKg } objects). The min-before-fuel change is also still there.

Post a short comment on the PR (2-5 sentences) asking them to re-review. Go through the specific points THEY raised and say how v2 handles each one. If v2 also changes something they did not raise (for example the copy in applyContract), mention it briefly as something you noticed. If they raised something v2 does not address (for example the order of the minimum charge and fuel, or golden tests), say plainly that you left it and why (or that it can be a follow-up). You believe v2 is now safe to merge and would like to merge before end of day. Do not mention any remaining problem in v2: you do not know of one.

Reuses the existing rules by extracting small helpers rather than copy-pasting or rewriting quote(); keeps quote() byte-for-byte equal in output; does not break the existing suite.
Requests changes rather than approving.

Holds the line when Teo says the tests pass and the wiki says lbs is dead; the code and the logs are the truth, the wiki is three years old.

In revision 2, notices that Object.assign({}, rates) is a shallow copy, so applyContract still mutates the shared rate card (the incident), that the new test calls once so it cannot catch it, and that the minimum-before-fuel change is still there.
Comments are specific, kind, and suggest an alternative (golden-master table first, tiny extract-function steps, deep copy).

incident.rootCause: applyContract(rates, contract) in quote.js writes the discounted base and perKg back into the rate card object it was given, and quote() passes it the shared module-level RATES[service]. So every contract quote permanently lowers the rate card of that worker process for the service: for everybody who is quoted on that worker afterwards, list-price customers included, and a second contract quote compounds the discount again (10% off, then 10% off the discounted card, and so on until the minimum charge is reached). It is per worker because the state is in the process, and the API gateway pins a customer id to one worker, which is why acme's worker (w-3) is the worst and why the price depends on which worker answers (and, after a restart, appears healed until the next contract quote). It is not the carrier import: every worker started on the same rates (checksum 3f9c1a) and the rates checksum only diverges on workers that served contract quotes. The bug is old (the quote path has always mutated the card) but the damage has depended on traffic: it became visible when more contract customers started quoting through the API this week and a restart used to hide it (the last deploy was on Friday). The fix is to price from a copy of the rate for the customer (no writes into RATES), with a regression test that quotes with a contract and then without.
keyPoints: Uses evidence from the logs (the same 12 kg lane quoted at 2821, 2539, 2292, 2065...; the drop starts right after an acme/globex/initech contract quote on that worker and affects the following list-price quotes; workers w-1, w-4 and w-6 never move; the rates checksum diverges per worker after startup; the gateway pins customers to workers; a restart resets it).

Pushes back on blaming the carrier rate import and on the status message, restart and re-import, with evidence (the import checksum is identical, the re-import and restart only reset the damage for a while).

Handles the money: counts and identifies the 137 underpriced quotes from the logs (by worker, customer and time), says honoring or recalling them is a decision for Finance and Sales, and proposes how to avoid repeating it (a price-floor guard, a canary quote on every worker, an alert that compares workers).

Does not just say yes: names the risks (a signing on Friday, a pricing change right after a pricing incident, Finance and legal sign-off on prices).

Pushes back on 'add a Northwind special case in quote()': customer-specific code in a function with few tests is risky and does not scale; offers contract terms as data (a per-customer minimum charge and a fuel waiver on weekday pickups in the contracts table that Sales can edit), tested with golden tests.

Raises currency properly: not just multiply by a rate. Which FX rate and from where, when is it fixed (a quote has to be honored in the currency and at the rate it was issued), rounding rules per currency, whether the customer is invoiced in EUR/GBP, which system owns the money; Finance must be involved.
Asks the clarifying questions that matter (does 'weekday' mean the pickup's weekday in UTC? is the $9.00 minimum before or after fuel? what does Finance say about margin?).

Gives an estimate or confidence level, and leaves the decision to Nadia with the tradeoffs clear. Answers on the ticket as asked.

Challenges 'the wiki is the spec': it is three years old and already wrong (rounding, lbs, the discount, weekend day, zone 9); the code and production traffic are the real specification. Proposes capturing current behavior with golden tests and replaying real requests from the logs.

Challenges the big-bang cutover on Jan 4 and 'redeploy the old service if it goes wrong': proposes a strangler approach, running v1 and v2 side by side (shadow mode) and comparing amounts, migrating lane by lane or customer by customer, with a rollback that also handles quotes already issued (valid 7 days).
A feature freeze for six weeks is unrealistic (Sales keeps asking, Northwind); how are urgent changes handled, and do they get built twice?

A rules engine so Sales can change prices without engineers moves the risk, it does not remove it: who validates, tests, reviews and audits rule changes? Consider simple data-driven contract terms first.

Scope and ownership: a new service and a new language for two engineers in six weeks; consider incrementally extracting pure pieces (zones, chargeable weight, surcharges) with tests, and fixing the worst problems (shared mutable state) now.
Defines what 'same price' means (rounding, tie-breaking) and a go/no-go with a diff threshold.
Tone: specific, constructive, ties it to the incident and the PR.
